Evan (Acme): hey team — we started seeing a spike of 429s this morning during our batch ingestion window. avg qps is low but bursts hit ~200 concurrent requests for ~30s. using continuous batching + KV cache. logs show a lot of Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining going to 0. any ideas?

Maya - Support Eng: sorry you're hitting that, can you paste an example request id or a raw curl? also which model and plan/account id?

Evan (Acme): request id: req_8f3a2b, account: acme-inc-42, model: redwood-7b-v2, client: node-sdk v2.3. payloads are short prompts (~40 tokens) but we intentionally flood for small bursts. here's a sample header block from one 429: `X-RateLimit-Limit: 600/min`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0`, `Retry-After: 12`. we also see `x-rw-quota-reset: 2025-11-09T14:23:00Z` sometimes.

Ben - SRE: quick thought — continuous batching can introduce request coalescing that looks like a sudden burst upstream, even if avg qps is low. if many clients' micro-batches flush simultaneously the rate limiter sees a concentrated spike. do you have client concurrency and max latency config?

Evan (Acme): client concurrency = 80, we set max_batching_latency_ms to 20, batch_size cap = 64. KV cache is enabled with per-session keys (we do prefix caching).

Maya - Support Eng: thanks. couple of things to check: 1) Are you using a shared key namespace so cache misses cause lots of identical requests to hit the model at once (cache stampede)? 2) Are your clients retrying aggressively on 429 with zero jitter? 3) The hosted plan enforces per-account and per-route token/min quotas — bursts can exhaust the per-minute window even if hourly averages look fine.

Evan (Acme): we do jitter on retries but it was low (100ms). and yes the cache key uses `user_id` + conversation prefix, which might not be ideal for deduping.

Maya - Support Eng: ok. repro steps we want: - run your burst script with concurrency 80 and batch latency 20ms - capture response headers and a few request ids - try again with batch latency 5ms and concurrency 40 to compare

Evan (Acme): repro snippet (node):
```js
// simple repro
const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.RW_KEY });
async function fire(n) {
  await Promise.all(Array.from({length:n}).map(() => client.generate({model:'redwood-7b-v2',prompt:'hi',max_tokens:20})));
}
fire(80);
```

Ben - SRE: couple of immediate recommendations: - lower client concurrency to spread arrivals (40-50) - increase max_batching_latency_ms to 50-100ms so the runtime can smooth bursts into larger, fewer batches - implement cache warming or a mutex around cache population to avoid stampedes - ensure exponential backoff + jitter on 429s (start ~500ms)

Priya - AM: Evan — we can also temporarily bump your burst quota/limit on the hosted plan while you tune. ping me if you'd like a one-time increase.

Evan (Acme): appreciate that. curious — if we move to Dedicated would this behavior go away? is it per-account limiter or global?

Maya - Support Eng: Dedicated gives you reserved capacity so you won't be affected by other tenants' load. however you still need to manage client-side burst patterns and batching; continuous batching behavior is same but you control GPU pool sizing and per-deployment concurrency. Per-account rate limits on hosted are enforced to protect shared capacity.

Ben - SRE: also watch the KV cache semantics: if your cache key granularity is too fine (per-session) you get many misses. consider a two-tier key: a stable prefix for common context + session suffix only when needed, or use prefix/KV TTL to let warm cache absorb initial load.

Evan (Acme): ran the smaller test: concurrency 40 + batching latency 80ms -> no 429s in 10 runs. with 80 concurrency + 20ms we get 429s within ~10s. that points to rate-limiter seeing concentrated bursts.

Maya - Support Eng: that's a good signal. next we want to see headers for a failing request — if X-RateLimit-Remaining goes negative or Reset timestamp jumps that indicates per-minute window exhaustion. can you paste one failing response headers?

Evan (Acme): here's a failing response header dump: 
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Date: Sun, 09 Nov 2025 14:22:49 GMT
X-RateLimit-Limit: 600/min
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1700007769
Retry-After: 12
X-Request-Id: req_8f3a2b
```

Ben - SRE: perfect — Reset looks like a unix epoch. The host-side limiter is per-account per-route per-minute. Two mitigation ideas: 1) smoothing at client side (spread requests over 60s) 2) enable a small local coordinating queue that batches and schedules sends so you don't overwhelm the minute window.

Maya - Support Eng: I'll open internal ticket INF-4421 for runtime to look at whether our batching flush heuristics + rate limiter can be tuned to avoid penalizing short bursts when KV cache warms. we'll attach your repro and headers.

DeployBot: Deployment successful: runtime-patch/allow-soft-burst INF-4421 applied to canary clusters at 2025-11-09T16:10:12Z :sparkles:

Priya - AM: updating you — I've provisioned a temporary +25% burst allowance on your hosted account for 24h (acme-inc-42). should help while you test.

Evan (Acme): thanks team — after lowering concurrency and increasing batch latency the window looks stable. one follow-up: is there a recommended pattern for caching when using continuous batching?

Maya - Support Eng: yes — recommended pattern: - use coarse-grained cache keys for shared context, TTL 60s-5m for warm caches - when populating cache, guard with a single-flight pattern (mutex) so only one upstream call happens - prefer idempotent prompt hashing as key when prompts are identical - for interactive chat, consider per-conversation KV with prefix fallback to reduce misses

Ben - SRE: and instrument client-side metrics: per-second requests, batch sizes distribution, retry counts. that will help tune both batching and quotas.

Evan (Acme): noted. we'll implement mutex + backoff and rerun. thanks for quick turnaround.

Maya - Support Eng: leaving this open until you confirm final results — tagging infra/eng-runtime. feel free to DM if you hit anything else. :thumbsup:
